context_blurb:
Nearly every cell holds DNA, a long molecule that spells out genes in four chemical letters. To use a gene, a cell copies it into a working message, then turns the message into a protein, a molecule that builds and runs the body.

Many biologists thought genes were protein. In 1952 Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase checked with a phage, a virus of bacteria made of DNA inside a protein coat. Sulfur is in protein but not DNA, and phosphorus the reverse, so radioactive sulfur marked the coats and radioactive phosphorus the DNA. They let the phages infect bacteria, then blended off the empty coats. Had protein been the genes, the sulfur would have turned up inside the bacteria and the phosphorus outside. Instead most phosphorus went in and most sulfur stayed out: genes are DNA.

DNA's four letters are bases: A, T, G and C. Around 1950 Erwin Chargaff found human DNA held A and T near three tenths each and G and C near a fifth. Only one pairing of bases across the two strands fits such figures: A with T, and G with C. Facing bases must come in equal amounts.

Watson and Crick built that pairing into their 1953 double helix, two strands wound round each other, helped by Photo 51, an X-ray picture of DNA taken by Rosalind Franklin and Raymond Gosling, her student; its dark cross showed a helix. As she prepared to leave King's College London, Gosling passed it to Maurice Wilkins. When James Watson visited King's in January 1953, Wilkins showed it to him without telling her. Nothing was taken from her desk, but she was not asked. Franklin died in 1958, four years before Watson, Crick and Wilkins shared a Nobel Prize, which is never given to the dead.

Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl then tested how DNA copies. They made bacterial DNA heavy with heavy nitrogen, let it copy once on ordinary nitrogen, and spun it in a tube that sorts by density. If old helices stayed whole beside all-new copies, the tube would show two bands, heavy and light, in equal amounts. Instead one band sat midway. So the strands part, each a template, or pattern, for a new partner.

The message is messenger RNA, read by ribosomes, the cell's protein builders. It is built along one DNA strand, each RNA base pairing with the base opposite: A with T, G with C, C with G, and U with A, as RNA uses uracil, U, in place of thymine. So a strand reading TAC-GGA yields the messenger A-U-G-C-C-U.

Two-letter words from four bases give only 16, too few for the twenty amino acids of proteins; three-letter words give 64. In 1961 Francis Crick, Sydney Brenner and colleagues added bases to a phage gene with the chemical proflavin. One or two extra bases shifted how every later base was grouped, garbling the gene. With three, the bases between the additions were misread, then reading fell back into step and the protein worked. So a gene is read in words of three bases, from a fixed start, without overlap.

That year Marshall Nirenberg and Heinrich Matthaei gave a protein-building juice from bacteria an artificial messenger of pure U, with all twenty amino acids. It built only phenylalanine. Since genes are read in threes, the messenger said U-U-U over and over, so U-U-U is the code word for phenylalanine.

Haemoglobin is the oxygen-carrying protein of red blood cells. In 1956 Vernon Ingram cut normal and sickle-cell haemoglobin into pieces with trypsin, an enzyme that cuts proteins, and sorted them into spots; one spot differed. That piece held one amino acid in place of another: valine where glutamic acid belongs. He was the first to show that one changed amino acid can cause a disease.

In 1983 Kary Mullis invented PCR, a way to copy a chosen stretch of DNA over and over. Each round begins with heat, which parts the two strands of each helix. As the tube cools, an enzyme builds a partner along each strand, so one helix becomes two, then four.

In 1984 Alec Jeffreys found DNA fingerprints, band patterns unique to each person. A current pulls cut DNA, which is negatively charged, through a gel toward the positive end. Charge grows with length, so in plain liquid all sizes move alike. But a gel is a tangle of fibres, a sieve, and the gel's mesh holds long pieces back more, so short ones run farther.
